kurz: Why the order of returns determines the outcome when you withdraw money, what the 4% rule really says, and how required minimum distributions and the tax order of your accounts shape the withdrawal plan.

bloecke.md: An investor who invests a sum once and neither pays in nor withdraws anything for 30 years reaches the same final value regardless of whether the bad years came at the beginning or at the end, because the order does not matter when the annual returns are multiplied. As soon as money is withdrawn, this no longer applies. When money is withdrawn in a loss year, shares are sold at a low price, and these shares are permanently missing in the recovery. Almost everything that distinguishes a withdrawal strategy from a savings plan follows from this difference. It is also the reason why there is no simple answer to the question “how much can I take out each year”.

## Origin of the 4% rule

In 1994, in the *Journal of Financial Planning*, William Bengen examined which real withdrawal a US portfolio of stocks and bonds would have sustained for 30 years in any starting year since 1926. He arrived at around 4% of the starting assets in the first year. This amount is then increased each year in line with [[Inflation|inflation]], regardless of how the portfolio performs. The so-called Trinity study by Cooley, Hubbard and Walz (1998) re-examined the same question in terms of a probability of success for different stock allocations and withdrawal periods. Its tables have been cited ever since.

Both studies are methodologically sound. In everyday use, however, their results are often misrepresented.

- The 4% figure does not refer to the current portfolio value at any given time. The percentage is applied only once, in the first year. After that, the withdrawal is a fixed dollar amount adjusted for inflation, which no longer depends on the portfolio value. With starting assets of $500,000, that is $20,000, even if the portfolio falls to $300,000.
- The rule does not guarantee success; it states a success rate. In the tables, “success” only meant that more than zero was left after 30 years. Even a portfolio in which only $4,000 remains after 30 years counts as a success.
- The results apply before costs and before tax. The calculations used index series, without fund expenses, advisory fees or income taxes. Whether $20,000 withdrawn from a traditional IRA, a Roth IRA or a taxable account leaves $20,000 or considerably less to spend depends on the account.
- The rule is based on US data. In the 20th century, American stocks and bonds performed better than those in most other developed countries.

For US investors, too, the last point matters. In 2010, Wade Pfau repeated the calculation using the long-term series of Dimson, Marsh and Staunton for 17 countries. In only a few of them, including the US, Canada and Denmark, would a real withdrawal of 4% historically have lasted for 30 years. Germany, Japan, Italy and France were well below this; in Germany and Japan, war and inflation destroyed most nominal wealth within a few decades, and bonds, which serve as a buffer in the US calculation, lost most of their value. The 4% figure is therefore the result of the most successful major market of the century. Adopting it as a universally valid figure means assuming that the next 30 years will be as good for US markets as the best historical periods were.

## Sequence-of-returns risk

[[Sequence-of-returns risk]] can be shown without a simulation. Two portfolios each start with $500,000, and $20,000 is withdrawn from each at the end of every year. Both experience the same five annual returns, only in reverse order: minus 20%, minus 10%, plus 5%, plus 25% and plus 30%. Without withdrawals, both portfolios would reach the same amount of $614,250. With withdrawals, this is not the case.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with $500,000 starting assets and a $20,000 withdrawal at the end of each year; after five years, the two portfolios are $58,918 apart purely because of the order of returns.

bloecke.md: The first five to ten years of retirement largely determine how things develop afterwards. A crash at 65 has a different effect from the same crash at 85. In the first case, 25 more withdrawals have to be paid from the shrunken capital afterwards, in the second only five.

## Withdrawal rules and their trade-offs

Every withdrawal rule weighs two goals against each other: an income that is as stable as possible and the lowest possible probability that the capital is used up before the end of life. The two goals cannot both be maximized at the same time.

bloecke.md: With the fixed real withdrawal, the risk that the capital runs out is greatest. At the same time, it is the only rule that continues to pay out unchanged even when prices fall sharply. With the fixed percentage withdrawal, the capital cannot run out. In return, the withdrawal falls with the market, so after a 40% decline, income also falls by 40%. Withdrawing the required minimum distribution each year is a variant of the percentage rule whose percentage rises with age. The rules in the following sections lie between these approaches.

## The Guyton and Klinger guardrails

In 2006, Jonathan Guyton and William Klinger published a set of rules that changes the fixed withdrawal only when the current [[Withdrawal rate|withdrawal rate]] leaves a corridor around the starting rate. The withdrawal rate is the annual withdrawal divided by the current portfolio value. A corridor of ±20% is usual; with a starting rate of 4%, the guardrails are therefore at 4.8% and 3.2%. Under an additional inflation rule, the inflation adjustment is skipped if the portfolio return in the previous year was negative.

The portfolio starts with $500,000 and a withdrawal of $20,000, that is, 4.0%. The guardrails are at 4.8% and 3.2%.

First, the portfolio slumps to $350,000.

1. Because of the negative year, the inflation rule means there is no increase; the withdrawal stays at $20,000 instead of $20,600.
2. The current rate of 20,000 ÷ 350,000 = 5.71% is above the upper guardrail.
3. The capital preservation rule cuts the withdrawal by 10% to $18,000; the new rate is 5.14%.

The rule cuts only once a year. If the portfolio stays low, the withdrawal is cut again the following year. The adjustment is deliberately sluggish so that a single bad quarter does not trigger a panic decision.

The portfolio then recovers to $620,000.

The rate of 18,000 ÷ 620,000 = 2.90% is now below the lower guardrail. The withdrawal is increased by 10% to $19,800 (3.19%). Two years later, $200 of the $2,000 cut still remains.

A second approach makes the rate depend on market valuation rather than on your own portfolio value. The basic idea is that people who retire when markets are highly valued have worse starting conditions and should therefore withdraw less.

bloecke.erklaerung: The rule derives the withdrawal rate from the CAPE. The reciprocal 1/CAPE is the cyclically adjusted earnings yield of the market. The rate rises when stocks are cheap and falls when they are expensive.

bloecke.md: The coefficients a and b are not derived from theory. They were fitted to the same historical series from which the 4% rule also comes. A formula whose parameters were fitted to past data says no more about the future than the past itself. What is robust about the idea is the direction (expensive market, lower rate), less so the exact numerical value.

## Effect of a cash buffer

The most common measure against sequence risk is a buffer covering two to three years of needs in a high-yield savings account, a money market fund or short-term Treasury bills. In crash years, withdrawals are taken from this buffer instead of selling stocks. The buffer helps, but for a different reason from the one usually given.

Arithmetically, a buffer is an increased cash allocation. A portfolio with 88% stocks and 12% cash that is rebalanced annually behaves practically the same whether or not you call the 12% a “buffer”. With [[Rebalancing|rebalancing]], sales are made from the overweight asset class anyway, so after a crash they automatically come from bonds and cash rather than from stocks. The benefit of the buffer lies in behavioral economics. A visibly separate account that covers the withdrawals for three years reduces the likelihood of selling stocks after all when prices are at their low.

The portfolio amounts to $600,000, and the annual requirement from the portfolio is $24,000. A buffer of three years' requirements amounts to $72,000, that is, 12% of the assets.

If the expected return on the stock portion is four percentage points above the interest rate on cash, the buffer costs 12% × 4 points = 0.48 percentage points a year on total assets, around $2,880 in the first year. This cost is not zero, but it can be quantified, and it is considerably smaller than the damage caused by a panic sale.

## Which account the money comes from

In the US, the tax on a withdrawal depends less on whether you sell or receive a distribution than on the account it comes from. From a *taxable brokerage account*, only the gain portion of the shares sold is taxable; the cost basis comes back tax-free. Long-term gains and qualified dividends are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% under 26 U.S.C. § 1(h). From a *traditional* 401(k) or IRA, every dollar withdrawn is ordinary income, because the contributions were never taxed. From a *Roth* IRA, qualified withdrawals after age 59½ and five years are tax-free. A dividend in a taxable account is taxed in full, even if economically it partly just returns capital; a sale of the same amount is taxed only on its gain portion.

The assumptions are a marginal tax rate of 22% and a long-term capital gains rate of 15%.

- Taxable account, sale with a 60% gain portion: gain $14,400 × 15% = $2,160 tax.
- Traditional IRA: $24,000 × 22% = $5,280 tax.
- Roth IRA, qualified withdrawal: no tax.

In the 12% bracket, long-term gains usually fall into the 0% band; the sale from the taxable account is then tax-free, while the IRA withdrawal still costs 12%. A dividend of $15,000 would cost $2,250 at 15%; a sale of the same amount with a 60% gain portion costs $1,350. The difference is smaller than the difference between the accounts.

bloecke.unter: From a taxable account at a 15% capital gains rate, the tax rises with the gain portion of the shares sold; even with an 80% gain portion, it is only 12% of the withdrawal. From a traditional IRA, the full amount is taxed at the marginal rate, here 22%.

bloecke.md: In a taxable account, you can choose the gain portion. Brokers apply first in, first out by default, so the oldest shares with the highest gains are sold first. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.1012-1(c), however, you may identify specific lots at the time of sale, for example those with the highest cost basis. The cost basis method has to be set or specified before the trade; afterwards, it cannot be changed.

## Required minimum distributions

Tax-deferred accounts cannot be deferred forever. Under 26 U.S.C. § 401(a)(9) as amended by the SECURE 2.0 Act, required minimum distributions (RMDs) from traditional IRAs, 401(k)s and similar plans start at age 73 for people born from 1951 to 1959 and at 75 for those born in 1960 or later. The first RMD may be postponed until April 1 of the following year, but then two RMDs fall into the same tax year. If an RMD is missed, an excise tax of 25% of the shortfall applies, reduced to 10% if it is corrected in time. Roth IRAs have no RMDs during the owner's lifetime, and since 2024 neither do Roth accounts in employer plans. The RMDs of several IRAs can be taken from any one of them; those of 401(k) plans must be taken from each plan separately.

bloecke.md:
## Order of withdrawals

The conventional order is first the taxable account, then the tax-deferred accounts, and the Roth accounts last, so that the tax-advantaged money keeps growing for as long as possible. Strictly followed, however, this order wastes the low brackets. In the years between the end of work and the start of Social Security and RMDs, many retirees have hardly any taxable income. If they live only on the taxable account, they pay little tax in these years, and later the RMDs, together with Social Security, push them into the 22% or 24% bracket, make up to 85% of the benefits taxable and possibly trigger Medicare surcharges.

The alternative is to fill the low brackets deliberately each year: withdraw from the traditional IRA or convert to Roth up to the top of the 12% bracket, for example, and take the rest from the taxable account, where long-term gains often stay in the 0% band. The exact optimum depends on the size of the accounts, the claiming age for Social Security, the tax rates of the heirs and the state. The principle is to spread taxable income over as many years as possible instead of letting it pile up later.

bloecke.titel: Taxes and RMDs are not handled automatically
bloecke.md:
In retirement, no employer withholds tax. Federal income tax on Social Security, IRA withdrawals and investment income has to be paid during the year, either through withholding or through quarterly estimated payments on Form 1040-ES. Withholding can be requested on Form W-4V for Social Security (7%, 10%, 12% or 22%) and on Form W-4R for IRA distributions; a nonperiodic IRA distribution has 10% withheld by default unless you choose otherwise, and a 401(k) distribution paid to you that could be rolled over has 20% withheld. To avoid an underpayment penalty, you generally have to pay at least 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's (110% if your adjusted gross income was above $150,000). Withholding counts as paid evenly over the year no matter when it was taken, so a withdrawal in December with a high withholding rate can cover the tax for the whole year.

The RMD must be withdrawn by December 31 even if prices have just fallen. It does not have to be sold, however: shares can be transferred in kind to a taxable account. They are taxed at their market value, but the investment stays in place.

bloecke.unter: The routine consists of one appointment in January, one calculation and three possible outcomes; afterwards only the account from which the money comes has to be decided.

bloecke.md:
The classic studies use real historical time series and run through every possible starting year once. This preserves relationships that a random number generator does not capture, such as the reversion of valuations to the mean, the link between inflation and bond yields, and real crash patterns. The disadvantage is the thin data basis. With 100 years of history, there are only just over 70 overlapping 30-year windows, and these overlap so much that they are not independent observations.

A [[Monte Carlo simulation]], by contrast, generates any number of paths from an assumed distribution. This produces smooth probabilities, which, however, reflect exactly the assumptions that were fed into the model. If a normal distribution without autocorrelation is assumed, extreme years are too rare and recovery phases too weak. A success rate of “94%” from a calculator therefore describes a property of the model and not a probability. It is useful as a measure for comparing two rules, not as an absolute statement.

- Choose a starting rate below 4% if costs and taxes still have to be paid from the withdrawals or if retirement could last longer than 30 years.
- Set down a rule in writing before the first crash comes. The guardrails only work if they are fixed in advance.
- Cover the expenses you cannot do without (housing, insurance, food) from secure sources, that is, from Social Security and, where applicable, a pension or an [[Immediate annuity|immediate annuity]]. Only the remaining part of the expenses should depend on the capital market.
- Schedule the January appointment firmly in order to note the account values, calculate the rate, plan the RMD, the withholding and any Roth conversion, and check whether your income will cross a threshold for the taxation of Social Security or for Medicare surcharges.

mitnehmen: In the withdrawal phase, the order of returns determines the outcome alongside the average return; in the example, the same five years in reverse order led to a difference of $58,918.
The 4% rule is based on US data before costs and taxes; internationally, only a few markets would have sustained this rate, and the US was the exception rather than the rule.
Rules with guardrails trade moderate fluctuations in income for greater security of capital; cuts are made only when the current rate leaves the corridor.

The tax on a withdrawal depends mainly on the account: from a taxable account only the gain portion at 0%, 15% or 20%, from a traditional IRA every dollar at the marginal rate, from a Roth IRA nothing.
RMDs from 73 or 75 force taxable withdrawals; filling low brackets in the years before, and paying tax through withholding or estimated payments, belong in the annual plan.

begriffe.text: Highest share of the starting assets that could be withdrawn, adjusted for inflation, over a fixed period without the capital being used up before the end of the period in any historical starting year. It is also known as SAFEMAX or the safe withdrawal rate.

Limits set around the initial withdrawal rate, usually ±20%. If the current rate leaves this corridor, the withdrawal is cut or increased by a fixed percentage. The guardrails form the central part of the set of rules by Guyton and Klinger (2006).

Price divided by the inflation-adjusted average earnings of the past ten years, also called CAPE. The ratio smooths out business cycles and serves as a valuation measure from which valuation-based withdrawal rules derive their rate.

Amount that must be withdrawn each year from traditional IRAs and employer plans from age 73 (75 for people born in 1960 or later). It equals the previous year-end balance divided by the factor from the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table and is taxed as ordinary income.
Transfer from an IRA directly to a charity from age 70½ under 26 U.S.C. § 408(d)(8). It counts towards the RMD and is not included in taxable income, up to an annual limit adjusted for inflation.

The risk of living longer than your own capital lasts. Withdrawal rules can limit it. It can only be handed over completely through a lifelong payment, such as Social Security or an annuity, which comes at the expense of flexibility and of being able to leave an inheritance.
